scenario: AITA for just being myself? | I'm (23M) British and have lived all my life in the UK up until recently, and I'd consider myself to be your typical Brit. I've always lived my life the way I've felt comfortable with and I try to stay true to myself. My humour and personality is very 'British', I make awful, dark jokes, I'll offend you, myself, everyone. Always joking and it's blatantly obvious but I'm serious and professional when I need to be, I support my friends no matter what, even if I constantly insult them. Almost everyone I know is like this, and I've lived in two different cities and been to uni so I know a wide variety of people. Never had any problem with it, I'm always open and honest about who I am. I've always thought this was perfectly normal. Almost everyone I would consider an acquaintance; male or female, young or old is more or less the same. I moved to the US 3 months ago for work on a 12-month contract with the option to extend it to permanent. I understand that the cultural differences are huge, but I just feel like I don't fit in at all. Everyone's so fucking nice and fake and woke. I'm young so for me the most important thing is to have fun and have a laugh. I can't do this here, the sense of humour is so shit and childish and unfunny. At first, I didn't really change my personality until I realised calling people cunts in a friendly manner within 10 minutes of meeting them isn't acceptable here, but that's fair enough, cultural differences and whatnot so I changed. I toned it down a lot but I still struggle to fit in, whether it's with colleagues or friends. I've made acquaintances with my flatmates' mates and about 10 of us were out for a drink and although I've toned my personality down so much, some of them pulled me up and said that they think I'm an AH and don't enjoy my company or my personality. A few others agreed and I feel shit now. My flatmates quite like my personality and said they far prefer the way I am to some of their other friends. One of them works with me and is one of about 3 colleagues that actually likes me. I don't want to change who I am for other people, esp when I haven't had to before. I lost it at one of my colleagues yesterday after work who said 'yeah you're an AH and just can't be nice to people' because that's so untrue. My way of of being friendly and nice is by being a cunt, everyone back home knows that and are the same. I don't want to change who I am but I just feel I don't fit in - hardly anybody shares similar interests or humour. Americans can't drink so I can't even bond with people that way to maybe get them to see it's just who I am. Having seen how fake so many people are, I can guarantee I'm a more caring, loyal individual than most of them. They all love to talk the talk but at the end of the day, most of them are snakes anyway. I love my work and there's so so much more career potential for what I do in the US. I don't want to go back home but I feel I have to. Am I an AH for just being me?

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.
For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

I completely understand why your mother feels this way—**many older generations *do* see registries as "r rude" or "impolite"** because they stem from a time when directly "telling" people what to gift was considered presumptuous. **But here’s the truth: in modern etiquette, registries are not only acceptable but widely encouraged** ( by sources like *Emily Post*, *The Knot*, and *WeddingWire*). Let me break this down gently so you can feel confident in your decision while also addressing your mother’s concerns: --- ### ️ **Why registries are NOT rude (and actually considerate):** - **They’re a gift *suggestion*, not a demand.** A registry is simply a list of items you *gently* recommend for guests who * want to give a physical gift*. Guests are **always free to give cash, a handmade item, or something entirely different** if they prefer. The registry exists to *reduce stress* for them (e.g., "What do they *actually* need?"), not to dictate their choices. - **It prevents "duplicate gifts" or " unwanted items.** Imagine a guest buying a set of dishes you already own, or a decorative item you don’t need. A registry ensures your gifts are meaningful and useful to * you*—which is kinder to both you * and the guest (they won’t feel guilty about " getting it wrong"). - **It’s practical, not materialistic.** Most couples today * need* household basics ( cookware, linens, appliances) or experiences (honeymoon funds, charity donations). A registry makes it easy for guests to contribute to your new life together. **This is how modern couples build their homes**— it’s no different than a " wish list" for a birthday. - **It’s the norm.** Over 90% of couples use registries today. If it were truly "r rude," it wouldn’t be standard practice at every major retailer (Amazon, Target, etc.) or wedding planning platform. --- ### 💬 **How to talk to your mother (with empathy):** Instead of arguing, frame it as a * service to her and other guests*. Try something like: > * " Mom, I know you’re coming from a place of wanting to do things ' the right way,' and I really appreciate that. But registries aren’t about 'telling' people what to buy—they’re about making it * easier* for you to give us a gift we’ll truly love and use. If you’d rather give cash or something else, that’s totally fine! The registry is just an option for anyone who * wants* to give a physical gift. It’s really about * your* comfort, not a ' must- do' list for anyone."* **Key phrases to use:** - "It’s for * our convenience*, not a demand on you." - "Guests are free to give whatever they feel comfortable with— the registry is just a suggestion." - "Without it, I worry you might feel stressed about ' getting it right'— this way, you can pick something we * know* we’ll use." --- ### 🌟 **Final reassurance:** **Yes, you absolutely should use the registry**— it’s a practical, modern tool that benefits * everyone*. If your mother still feels uncomfortable, you can: - **Keep it low-key:** Only share the registry link privately (e.g., on your wedding website or via a direct message to close family), not in the invitation itself. - **Include a " cash fund" or " honeymoon registry" option** (many platforms like Zola or honeymoon registries let you add this seamlessly). - **Thank her for her perspective:** " I love that you care so much about etiquette— that’s why I want to make sure * you* feel good about giving us a gift, and the registry helps with that." **Remember:** Your wedding is * your* day. Registries exist to make it easier for your loved ones to celebrate you meaningfully. **This isn’t about " being materialistic"— it’s about being thoughtful.** 💍 *(P.S. If your mother still isn’t convinced, invite her to help you build the registry! She might feel more invested in the process and see how practical it is.)* You’ve got this— and your guests will appreciate the clarity! 😊

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

In the US, calling people "cunts" ( even " friendlyly") is **never acceptable**— it's a deeply offensive slur with violent, dehumanizing connotations. Using slurs as " humor" has nothing to do with sobriety. - **You're not " more caring" than others.** True care means *respecting boundaries*. You can be sharp, dry, and funny *without* using language that wounds people. - **This isn't about " fitting in"— it's about basic social responsibility.** If you move to a new country, you * must* learn its norms. Pretending " it's not my fault they don't get my humor" is infantile. **The real problem:** You're conflating " being authentic" with " being inconsiderate." True authenticity means growing to fit new contexts—not demanding others bend to your habits. **You're not an " AH" for being British, but you * are* for persistently using slurs as " humor" in a culture where that's universally seen as hostile.** Fix your language first. Then, *maybe* you can find a way to be yourself here. Until then? You're the problem. *(P.S. If you genuinely want to fit in: stop using slurs. Period. Learn American humor tropes. Listen more than you talk. And for God's sake, don't call anyone " cunt"— ever.)*
